dossier.public_summary: Odd and even dips are completely different, with one sector showing a huge negative eclipse instead of the shallow 460 ppm dip, so the signal is not a stable planet transit. The shallow dip appears only in the QLP data and the star itself is strongly spotted and variable, best explained as a blend/variability artefact or false alarm rather than a planet.

reasons.why: Odd and even transits differ dramatically: one shows a deep ~-44k ppm eclipse, the even shows the shallow 460 ppm transit. A ~10 sigma difference favours an eclipsing binary at twice the reported period, not a planet.

Depth is wildly inconsistent between sectors, with the one outlier in sector 71 driving the apparent signal. Transit depths confirm it: negative depths -43874 ppm (sigma -11.0) and -29770 ppm (sigma -4.3) are not planet transits.
reasons.value: p_constant 0.001617; sector 71 depth_ppm -40398 err_ppm 14950 vs sectors 42 608 err_ppm 62, 43 443 err_ppm 52, 70 393 err_ppm 47

reasons.why: Tool shows the -40k ppm 'transit' is isolated to the QLP light curve in sector 71; SPOC products are steady at ~400-600 ppm, arguing the candidate depth itself is the noise/correction artefact causing the strange sign.

reasons.why: Star is a K dwarf with confirmed spot modulation (false_alarm 5.3184554555332505e-161, amplitude_ppm 2315) and transit density penalty 39.2, supporting large stellar variability that can create spurious dips and odd/even differences.
